vignette:
She is 66, a woman from Oceania, divorced for many years, and she runs a small neighborhood shop that she has owned long enough for people to measure parts of their lives against it. They tell her they bought school shoes there before their children grew up, or that her shelves still smell the same as they did when her husband was alive. She likes the ordinary rhythm of retail: lifting the shutters at dawn, lining up tins and packets, counting change, greeting regulars by name. Before everything changed, the shop gave her a sense of steadiness. She worked hard, kept mostly to herself, and took pride in being reliable.

The trouble begins late one evening two years ago, just after closing. There has been tension in the neighborhood over a reported theft nearby, and police cars have been moving up and down the street all week. She is pulling the metal shutter halfway down when officers stop in front of the shop. At first she assumes they want information. Instead, they begin shouting questions she does not understand, speaking over one another, accusing her of hiding someone inside. She tries to explain that she is alone, that she is closing for the night, but one officer pushes past her into the doorway. Another grabs her arm when she reaches toward the counter for her keys.

She remembers the feeling of being suddenly treated as if she is dangerous. She is a small older woman, wearing her apron, cash tray still open behind her, but none of that seems to matter. She says they twist her arms behind her back, press her against the counter, and force her to the ground when she cries out. Her cheek is against the cold tile. She can smell dust and spilled detergent. A knee is in her back. She cannot draw a full breath. She hears one of them say, “Stop resisting,” though in her mind she is not resisting at all; she is frightened and trying to protect her face. Customers gathering outside watch through the half-open shutter. Later, this part returns to her with particular cruelty: not only the pain, but the humiliation of being seen that way in her own shop, the place where she has always stood upright.

She is released without charges after hours of confusion and rough handling. No one explains much. In the following days, her wrists are bruised, her shoulder aches, and she tells neighbors she slipped and fell. What stays with her most is the shock. She cannot reconcile the woman she knows herself to be with the one the police seemed to see. At night she lies awake replaying the scene, trying to find the moment when it might have gone differently. The sound of boots on concrete, the metallic crash of the shutter, the officer’s voice—these repeat in her mind in jagged fragments. When she finally sleeps, she dreams that she is pinned and unable to call out.

She returns to the shop because she has to. It is her income, and she has no one else to run it. But the place no longer feels like hers. The corner near the counter, where she was forced down, becomes unbearable. She avoids looking at the floor tiles there. If a police vehicle passes, her body stiffens before she even consciously registers why. She begins leaving the shutter higher than before at closing time because the half-down position makes her heart race. When men enter speaking loudly, she loses track of what they are buying. Sometimes she smiles and serves them while inside she is counting exits, watching hands, listening for changes in tone.

Over time her world narrows. She stops staying open late. She no longer walks to the wholesale market before dawn; instead she pays extra for deliveries so she does not have to be alone on the street. She keeps the television on in the back room for noise, but any news about policing sends her into a spiral for hours. She startles violently if someone knocks unexpectedly. Once, when an officer enters the shop to buy bottled water, she freezes so completely that the customer behind him has to repeat herself three times. Afterward she locks the door and cries in the stockroom, ashamed of how her body seems to betray her.

Her divorce had taught her to rely on herself, and that self-reliance now hardens into isolation. Friends invite her to church events and family meals, but she often refuses, saying she is tired or busy with inventory. The truth is that being around people feels effortful; she cannot follow conversation when part of her mind is scanning for danger. She is irritable with suppliers, mistrustful of strangers, and then guilty for becoming someone she does not recognize. She says she used to be patient. Now she snaps at children for touching displays, then spends the evening hating herself for it.

In the present, she still opens the shop most mornings, though she sits closer to the door than she used to and keeps her keys in her pocket at all times. She watches the street through the front glass with a vigilance that exhausts her. Some days are manageable, almost normal. On others, a siren in the distance or the scrape of metal on metal is enough to pull her back into that night, and the shop seems to shrink around her. She says she feels as though the assault is not over, only interrupted, as if some part of her is still on the floor behind the counter waiting for permission to stand up.
